chapters.title: The Role of the Coach
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should understand:
The different roles they perform during a season.
How coaching responsibilities change across age groups.
The behaviours that create positive learning environments.
volunteerChecklist: What should every player improve today?
Do I have enough footballs and equipment?
Can I explain every drill in under two minutes?
What will I do if only half my players attend?
What will I do if it rains?
How will I finish training on a positive note?
Common Mistakes Made by New Coaches
Running too many drills in one session.
Spending too much time on fitness without a football.
Focusing on winning junior matches rather than player development.
Correcting every mistake instead of allowing players to solve problems.
Using drills that are too advanced for the group's skill level.
Standing in one location instead of continually observing players.
Forgetting to praise effort, communication and improvement.

sections.title: What Is Coaching?
sections.content:
Many people believe coaching simply involves selecting drills, choosing a team and instructing players during matches.
Effective coaching is far broader.
A coach is simultaneously:
Teacher
Leader
Organiser
Motivator
Role model
Communicator
Mentor
Planner
Problem solver
Learner
The best coaches rarely possess every answer. Instead, they continually observe, adapt and improve their own coaching just as they expect players to improve their football.

sections.title: The Purpose of Coaching
sections.content:
The primary purpose of coaching Australian Football is to improve players.
Improvement occurs in many forms.
Technical Development
Helping players execute football skills more effectively.
Examples include:
Kicking
Handballing
Marking
Tackling
Ground ball collection
Goal kicking
Tactical Development
Helping players understand the game.
Examples include:
Creating space
Defensive positioning
Ball movement
Transition
Decision making
Team structures
Physical Development
Helping players become more capable athletes through football-specific movement.
Examples include:
Running
Agility
Acceleration
Deceleration
Balance
Coordination
Repeat efforts
Mental Development
Helping players become confident thinkers.
Examples include:
Decision making
Resilience
Concentration
Composure under pressure
Confidence
Accountability
Social Development
Football is a team sport.
Great coaches deliberately develop:
Respect
Communication
Leadership
Inclusion
Teamwork
Responsibility
Sportsmanship

sections.title: The Coaching Pyramid
sections.content:
Successful coaching follows a clear hierarchy.
Level 1 – Enjoyment
Players who enjoy training return next week.
Without enjoyment there is no long-term development.
Level 2 – Engagement
Players learn when they are actively involved.
Training should maximise:
Ball touches
Decision making
Movement
Communication
Waiting in lines should be minimised.
Level 3 – Learning
Only after players are engaged can meaningful learning occur.
Learning involves:
New skills
Better decisions
Improved understanding
Increased confidence
Level 4 – Performance
Performance naturally improves when players consistently enjoy training and continue learning.
Winning games should be viewed as the consequence of successful player development—not the starting objective.

sections.title: Responsibilities of an AFL Coach
sections.content:
Every coach has responsibilities before, during and after training.
Before Training
The coach should:
Plan the session.
Check equipment.
Prepare the playing area.
Review previous training outcomes.
Understand the session objectives.
Consider player numbers.
Prepare modifications if required.
A well-planned session appears effortless to players because the preparation has already been completed.
During Training
The coach should:
Keep players active.
Observe constantly.
Encourage communication.
Provide concise instruction.
Correct mistakes positively.
Adapt drills when required.
Maintain a safe environment.
Reinforce effort as much as execution.
Players should spend significantly more time participating than listening.
After Training
Reflection is essential.
The coach should ask:
Did players enjoy training?
Did they improve?
Were the objectives achieved?
Which drill worked best?
Which drill should be changed?
Which players require additional support?
What should next week's session focus on?
The most successful coaches continually refine their sessions rather than repeating the same program indefinitely.

sections.title: The AFCRL Coaching Principles
sections.content:
Every drill, session and season plan within this library is built upon the following principles.
Principle 1 – Players Learn by Playing
Football should resemble football.
Drills should include realistic movement, decision making and communication whenever possible.
Principle 2 – Maximise Ball Contacts
More footballs.
Smaller groups.
Less waiting.
Greater repetition.
Principle 3 – Progress Before Pressure
Players should first understand a movement before performing it under increasing pressure.
A typical progression is:
Learn the movement.
Repeat the movement.
Perform while moving.
Perform under passive pressure.
Perform under active pressure.
Perform in game-like situations.
Principle 4 – Reward Good Decisions
A correct decision that is poorly executed often represents better learning than an excellent execution of the wrong decision.
Praise decision quality as well as technical execution.
Principle 5 – Coach the Individual Within the Team
Every player develops at a different rate.
Training should challenge every player without overwhelming them.
Principle 6 – Make Every Drill Purposeful
Every activity should answer one question:
"What part of football does this improve?"
If that question cannot be answered clearly, reconsider the activity.
Coaching Australian Football is far more than organising drills or selecting a team. A coach is responsible for creating an environment where players enjoy attending, feel safe to make mistakes, and improve over time.
The most successful coaches focus first on enjoyment, engagement and learning. Performance and results are built upon these foundations.
Every chapter and drill that follows in this library will reinforce these principles, ensuring coaches have a consistent framework for planning sessions, teaching skills and developing players at every stage of their football journey.

chapters.title: Understanding How Players Learn
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Understand how football skills are learned.
Recognise the different stages of skill development.
Select coaching methods appropriate to player ability.
Use questioning rather than constant instruction.
Create training environments that maximise learning.
Recognise when players are ready to progress to more difficult activities.
Build confidence while maintaining appropriate challenge.
One player seems to master a skill almost immediately.
A third performs perfectly at training but cannot reproduce the same skill during a match.
This does not necessarily mean one player is more talented than another.

Players improve through repeated exposure to challenges that are neither too easy nor too difficult. Effective coaches understand that improvement occurs through a combination of instruction, repetition, experimentation, feedback and game experience.
The coach's role is not to eliminate mistakes.
The coach's role is to create an environment where mistakes become learning opportunities.
aiDecisionRules: Beginners should receive high-repetition, low-pressure activities.
Developing players should experience increasing variability.
Advanced players should train under realistic match conditions.
If error rates become excessive, reduce complexity rather than repetition.
If success rates exceed approximately 90% for prolonged periods, increase challenge.
If players appear disengaged, modify constraints before introducing new drills.
Every training session should include opportunities for both technical practice and game-based decision making.

sections.title: What Is Learning?
sections.content:
Learning is a relatively permanent improvement in a player's ability to perform a skill or make an effective decision.
Temporary success does not always indicate learning.
For example:
A player may successfully hit ten stationary kicks during training but fail to execute the same kick during a match under pressure.
True learning has only occurred when the player can consistently reproduce the skill in different situations.
Learning should therefore be measured by adaptability rather than perfection.

sections.title: Performance vs Learning
sections.content:
Many coaches confuse good performance with genuine learning.
Performance
Learning
Short-term
Long-term
Often occurs during practice
Transfers to matches
Can be influenced by easy drills
Can be reproduced under pressure
Looks impressive
Produces consistent improvement
A player dominating an easy drill may not actually be improving.
Conversely, a player making frequent mistakes during a challenging activity may be learning rapidly.
Coaches should avoid judging development solely by what they observe during one training session.

sections.title: The Four Stages of Skill Learning
sections.content:
Most football skills develop through four broad stages.
Stage 1 – Unconscious Incompetence
The player does not yet understand what they are doing incorrectly.
Examples include:
Incorrect grip on the football.
Poor kicking approach.
Running into poor positions.
Not scanning before receiving.
At this stage:
Demonstrations are critical.
Instructions should be simple.
Success should be easy to achieve.
Stage 2 – Conscious Incompetence
The player understands the correct technique but cannot consistently perform it.
This stage often feels frustrating.
Players know what they should do but cannot yet execute it.
This is where many players improve the most.
The coach should:
Encourage persistence.
Avoid excessive correction.
Reinforce successful attempts.
Stage 3 – Conscious Competence
The player performs correctly but must actively think about each movement.
Performance slows slightly because concentration is high.
This stage requires:
Repetition.
Increasing pressure.
More game-like scenarios.
Stage 4 – Unconscious Competence
Execution becomes automatic.
Players can now:
Scan the field.
Communicate.
Make decisions.
Adapt under pressure.
Instead of thinking about kicking mechanics, attention shifts toward solving football problems.
This is the ultimate objective of training.

sections.title: Why Players Make Mistakes
sections.content:
Mistakes are not necessarily signs of poor coaching.
Common reasons include:
Lack of Understanding
The player does not know what to do.
Lack of Repetition
The player understands the skill but has insufficient practice.
Pressure
Opponents reduce available time and space.
Fatigue
Decision-making quality often declines before technical skill.
Anxiety
Players worried about making mistakes frequently become hesitant.
Information Overload
Too many coaching points prevent effective learning.
A player thinking about:
Foot position
Ball drop
Eyes
Follow through
Defender
Target
Teammates
cannot process every instruction simultaneously.
Keep coaching cues simple.

sections.title: The Coach's Learning Toolbox
sections.content:
Effective coaches use multiple methods rather than relying solely on instruction.
Demonstration
Show the movement.
Players often learn faster by watching than listening.
Where possible:
Demonstrate at game speed.
Demonstrate slowly.
Demonstrate from multiple angles.
Guided Discovery
Rather than providing every answer, ask questions.
Examples:
"What made that kick successful?"
"Where was the space?"
"What did you see before you handballed?"
This develops independent thinkers.
Trial and Error
Allow players to experiment.
Not every mistake requires immediate correction.
Sometimes allowing failure produces stronger learning.
Repetition
Quality repetition remains essential.
However, repetition should involve slight variations.
Different angles.
Different pressure.
Different targets.
Different decisions.
Feedback
Feedback should be:
Specific.
Immediate when appropriate.
Positive.
Actionable.
Instead of saying:
"Bad kick."
Say:
"Your eyes dropped before contact. Keep your head over the ball."

sections.title: Block Practice vs Random Practice
sections.content:
Block Practice
The same skill repeated continuously.
Example:
Thirty identical kicks over twenty metres.
Advantages:
Builds confidence.
Introduces technique.
Easy for beginners.
Disadvantages:
Does not resemble football.
Random Practice
Skills performed in changing situations.
Example:
Players receive different passes, different defenders, different decisions and different targets every repetition.
Advantages:
Better match transfer.
Improves decision making.
Develops adaptability.
Disadvantages:
More mistakes occur.
Coaching Recommendation
Player Level
Preferred Practice
Beginner
Mostly Block Practice
Developing
Mixed Practice
Advanced
Mostly Random Practice

sections.title: Constraints-Based Coaching
sections.content:
Players learn best when coaches manipulate the environment rather than constantly giving instructions.
Examples include:
Make the playing area smaller.
Reduce time.
Increase defenders.
Add more footballs.
Limit handballs.
Reward switching play.
Increase scoring options.
Instead of telling players to move faster...
Create a drill that rewards quick movement.
Players naturally discover better solutions.

sections.title: Game Sense Coaching
sections.content:
Australian Football is a decision-making sport.
Rather than isolated technical drills, Game Sense coaching asks players to solve football problems.
Example:
Instead of practising uncontested kicking for twenty minutes...
Play a small-sided game where accurate kicking creates scoring opportunities.
Players improve both skill execution and tactical understanding simultaneously.

sections.title: Feedback Frequency
sections.content:
One of the most common coaching mistakes is talking too much.
Research consistently shows players retain more when allowed time to process information independently.
Good coaches observe more than they speak.
A useful guideline is:
Observe.
Allow.
Question.
Then instruct if necessary.

sections.title: Recognising Readiness to Progress
sections.content:
A player is generally ready to increase difficulty when they consistently demonstrate:
Correct technique.
Good decisions.
Confidence.
Communication.
Awareness.
Consistency under current pressure.
Do not progress players simply because time has elapsed.
Progress them because performance demonstrates readiness.
Practical Example
Teaching handball.
Poor Progression
Stationary handball.
↓
Full match.
Effective Progression
Stationary handball.
↓
Walking handball.
↓
Running handball.
↓
Passive defender.
↓
Active defender.
↓
Two decisions.
↓
Small-sided game.
↓
Match simulation.
Each stage builds upon the previous one.
Volunteer Coach Tips
Remember these simple rules.
Show before you explain.
Keep explanations under two minutes.
Ask more questions than you answer.
Let players solve problems.
Praise effort and decision making.
Increase challenge gradually.
Expect mistakes.
Finish every activity with success.
Common Coaching Mistakes
Correcting every error.
Talking continuously.
Progressing drills too quickly.
Repeating identical drills every week.
Removing all pressure from activities.
Criticising mistakes instead of analysing them.
Expecting immediate perfection.
Comparing players against each other rather than against their own improvement.
Learning football is a continuous process rather than a single event. Players develop through repeated exposure to progressively more challenging situations where they are encouraged to think, adapt and make decisions.
The most effective coaches do not eliminate mistakes—they design environments where mistakes become valuable learning opportunities. By understanding how players acquire skills, volunteer coaches can build training sessions that develop confident, intelligent footballers capable of transferring their learning into match situations.

chapters.title: Player Development by Age

One of the greatest mistakes a coach can make is coaching every age group the same way.
An Under 8 player is not simply a smaller Under 18 player.
Children, adolescents and adults differ significantly in their physical development, attention span, emotional maturity, ability to process information and reasons for participating in football.
A training session that motivates an Under 18 squad may overwhelm an Under 10 team. Likewise, activities designed for young children may quickly disengage senior players.
Effective coaches understand where their players are in their development and adapt their coaching accordingly.
The aim of each stage is to prepare players for the next stage—not to rush them through it.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Effective coaching begins with understanding the players in front of you. Each age group has unique physical, cognitive and emotional characteristics that influence how training should be delivered.
Successful coaches resist the temptation to coach younger players like adults. Instead, they progressively build skills, decision making and game understanding through developmentally appropriate activities that prepare players for the next stage of their football journey.
The goal is not to accelerate development at every opportunity, but to ensure each player leaves every stage with the confidence, competence and enjoyment required to continue progressing throughout their football career.

chapters.title: Planning Effective Training Sessions
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Plan structured, purposeful and engaging training sessions.
Select drills that match the objectives of the session.
Balance skill development, decision making and game play.
Adapt sessions for varying player numbers, weather conditions and available space.
Evaluate whether a session has achieved its objectives.
The quality of a football training session is determined long before the first football is kicked.

Successful coaches do not arrive at training and decide what to do on the night. They prepare every activity in advance, understand why each drill has been selected and know how they will adapt if circumstances change.
A well-planned training session should feel seamless to players. Equipment is already organised, drills flow naturally from one activity to the next and the coach spends minimal time explaining.
Poor planning leads to long breaks, confusion, unnecessary waiting, reduced learning and frustrated players.
This chapter provides the framework used throughout the AFCRL for designing every training session, regardless of age group or competition level.
aiDecisionRules: Finish with competitive football where appropriate.

sections.title: The Purpose of Every Training Session
sections.content:
Every session must answer one simple question:
"What do I want every player to be better at when they leave tonight?"
If the answer is unclear, the session lacks direction.
A session should never be built around favourite drills. It should be built around specific learning outcomes.
Examples include:
Improve handball under pressure.
Develop forward entries.
Improve defensive communication.
Introduce switching play.
Improve ground ball technique.
Develop centre clearance structure.
Every activity during the session should contribute to that objective.

sections.title: The AFCRL Session Planning Model
sections.content:
Every session follows the same structure.
Stage
Purpose
Arrival
Prepare players mentally and physically
Warm-Up
Raise body temperature and prepare movement
Skill Development
Introduce or refine technical skills
Skill Under Pressure
Apply skills with increasing difficulty
Game Application
Replicate match situations
Conditioning (if required)
Develop football-specific fitness
Review
Reinforce learning and prepare for next session
This structure remains consistent across all age groups, although the proportion of time spent in each stage varies.

sections.title: The Golden Rules of Session Planning
sections.content:
Rule 1 – One Primary Theme
Every session should have one primary focus.
Examples:
Kicking
Handball
Ball Movement
Team Defence
Forward Craft
Ground Balls
Avoid trying to teach five major concepts in one evening.
Players remember fewer things than coaches say.
Rule 2 – Build from Simple to Complex
Progression should always occur.
For example:
Technique
↓
Movement
↓
Pressure
↓
Decision Making
↓
Game
Players should never be thrown directly into a complex activity before understanding the required skill.
Rule 3 – Football Before Fitness
Whenever possible, develop fitness through football.
Instead of:
10 x 100 metre sprints
Consider:
Continuous transition games.
Repeat contest drills.
Numbers-up games.
Wave drills.
Players develop football fitness while simultaneously improving skill and decision making.
Rule 4 – Keep Everyone Moving
Inactive players are not learning.
Whenever possible:
Split groups.
Use multiple stations.
Increase football numbers.
Reduce queue lengths.
Create continuous drills.
Aim for every player to touch the football every 20–30 seconds during skill activities.
Rule 5 – Finish with Football
Players should leave training feeling like footballers—not runners.
Whenever possible, conclude with a competitive football activity.
This reinforces learning while maintaining enjoyment.

sections.title: The Five Questions Every Coach Should Answer
sections.content:
Before every training session, answer the following:
1. What are we teaching?
State it in one sentence.
Example:
"Tonight we are improving our ability to move the football from defence to attack."
2. Why are we teaching it?
Examples:
We struggled exiting defensive 50.
We turned the football over too often.
Our transition speed was poor.
Players lacked communication.
3. How will we teach it?
List the drills.
Example:
Warm-Up
↓
Possession Grid
↓
Overlap Kicking Drill
↓
Wave Transition
↓
6 v 6 Ball Movement Game
↓
Full Ground Simulation
4. How will I know we improved?
Create measurable outcomes.
Examples:
Fewer turnovers.
Faster ball movement.
More successful switches.
Better communication.
Improved decision making.
5. What if something changes?
Always prepare alternatives.
What if:
It rains?
Only twelve players attend?
You lose half the oval?
The lights fail?
Equipment is missing?
Experienced coaches always have a backup plan.

sections.content:

↓

Every activity reinforces the previous one.

sections.title: Common Session Mistakes
sections.content:
Too Much Talking
Players cannot improve while standing still.
Aim for explanations under two minutes.
Demonstrate first.
Speak second.
Too Many Drills
Changing drills every five minutes wastes valuable learning time.
Fewer drills.
Better coaching.
Greater repetition.
Drills Without Purpose
Avoid asking:
"What should we do next?"
Instead ask:
"What activity best develops tonight's objective?"
Fitness at the Expense of Football
Players joined football to play football.
Whenever possible:
Condition with footballs.
Condition with decisions.
Condition through competition.
No Progression
Running six unrelated drills creates disconnected learning.
Each activity should build towards the next.

sections.title: Session Reflection
sections.content:
The best coaches evaluate every session.
Ask yourself:
Did players improve?
Were they engaged?
Did they enjoy training?
Did the drills flow?
Did I speak too much?
Did everyone receive enough footballs?
Would I run this session again?
What would I change?
Reflection creates better coaching.

Notice how every activity develops the same theme.
Great training sessions are not collections of random drills. They are carefully planned learning experiences where every activity contributes to a clearly defined objective.
By following the AFCRL Session Planning Model, coaches can confidently design engaging, purposeful and enjoyable training sessions for any age group or competition level. Consistent planning, thoughtful progression and regular reflection form the foundation of effective coaching and player development.

chapters.title: The AFCRL Drill Classification System
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Understand the AFCRL drill numbering system.
Quickly locate drills appropriate for their team.
Select drills based on age, skill level, player numbers and available equipment.
Understand the progression system used throughout the library.
Build complete training sessions using the drill database.
Adapt drills to suit changing conditions.
Understand how the AFCRL AI Coaching System searches and recommends drills.
One of the biggest frustrations for community coaches is finding the right drill at the right time.
Most coaching books organise drills into broad categories such as kicking, handball or fitness. While useful, this approach rarely answers the practical questions coaches ask before training.
We only have one football between every three players.
We have access to half the oval.
I want a high-intensity drill that develops defensive communication.
Traditional coaching manuals require coaches to search through dozens of pages before finding a suitable activity.
The AFCRL solves this problem through a comprehensive drill classification system.
Every drill in this library follows the same structure, allowing coaches—and eventually AI systems—to instantly identify the most appropriate activity for any situation.
aiDecisionRules: When recommending drills, the AFCRL AI Coaching System should prioritise:
Progression within the overall training session.
No drill should ever be recommended based on a single factor alone.

Do I have enough footballs and equipment?
Does it fit the available space?
Will every player be actively involved?
Can I explain it clearly in under two minutes?
Do I know how to progress or simplify it if required?

chapters.title: Coaching Communication and Effective Instruction
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Deliver clear, concise and effective instructions.
Communicate appropriately with different age groups.
Improve player understanding through demonstrations and questioning.
Adapt communication during training and on match day.
Develop players who think independently rather than relying on constant direction.
Communication is the most important coaching skill.
A coach may possess exceptional football knowledge, but if players do not understand the message, learning will not occur.

Many outstanding community coaches are not elite football tacticians. They succeed because they communicate clearly, create enjoyable environments and help players understand what they are trying to achieve.
Every interaction between a coach and a player influences learning.
Communication is not limited to giving instructions. It includes demonstrations, body language, questioning, listening, encouragement, corrections, feedback and even silence.
The best coaches know not only what to say, but when to say it and, equally importantly, when not to say anything at all.
aiDecisionRules: Limit coaching points to one or two at a time.
Provide specific rather than generic feedback.
Recommend short coaching cues that players can remember during competition.
Encourage independence rather than coach dependency.
Adapt communication style to player maturity and experience.
volunteerChecklist: ✓ Use one coaching point at a time.
Failing to explain the purpose of activities.
Speaking only to the most talented players.

sections.title: The Communication Cycle
sections.content:
Effective coaching communication follows a simple cycle.
Explain.
Demonstrate.
Observe.
Allow players to perform.
Provide feedback.
Repeat.
Many inexperienced coaches unintentionally interrupt this cycle by continually talking while players are attempting to learn.
Learning occurs through action, not lectures.

sections.title: The Two-Minute Rule
sections.content:
Players attend football training to play football.
As a general principle:
Initial drill explanations should take less than two minutes.
Mid-drill corrections should take less than thirty seconds.
Longer discussions should occur after the activity has finished.
If an explanation exceeds two minutes, ask yourself:
Am I providing too much information?
Could I demonstrate instead?
Could the players learn this by doing?

sections.title: The Demonstration Principle
sections.content:
Players remember what they see more effectively than what they hear.
Whenever introducing a new activity:
Explain the objective.
Demonstrate the movement.
Demonstrate the drill.
Begin immediately.
If possible, use players to demonstrate rather than coaching alone.
Demonstrate:
At normal speed.
At slow speed.
From multiple angles.

sections.title: One Coaching Point at a Time
sections.content:
One of the most common mistakes made by coaches is attempting to correct everything simultaneously.
Example:
A player misses a kick.
Poor feedback:
Keep your head down.
Shorten your steps.
Hold the ball differently.
Follow through.
Point your toe.
Watch the target.
The player remembers almost nothing.
Better feedback:
"Keep your head over the football."
Allow repetition.
Once this improves, coach the next point.
One correction.
Lots of repetition.
Then move on.

sections.title: Ask Before You Tell
sections.content:
Players become better decision makers when they are encouraged to think.
Instead of immediately providing answers, ask questions.
Examples:
"What did you notice?"
"What option was available?"
"Why did that work?"
"What would you change next time?"
"Where was the space?"
"Who was free?"
Questions develop football intelligence.
Instructions often develop dependence.

sections.title: Positive Communication
sections.content:
Positive coaching does not mean ignoring mistakes.
It means creating an environment where mistakes are accepted as part of learning.
Effective coaches correct errors while maintaining confidence.
Instead of saying:
"You're doing that wrong."
Try:
"Good effort. Next time, try getting your body behind the ball."
Players should finish corrections believing they can improve.

sections.title: The Feedback Sandwich – Use with Caution
sections.content:
Many coaches are taught:
Positive.
Correction.
Positive.
While this approach has value, players quickly recognise insincere praise.
Instead, make all feedback genuine.
Example:
"I like your decision to take the game on. Keep doing that. The next step is lowering your body before collecting the football."
Specific feedback builds trust.
General praise often loses meaning.

sections.title: Individual vs Group Feedback
sections.content:
Not every correction should involve the whole team.
Use group instruction when:
Everyone is making the same mistake.
Safety is involved.
A tactical adjustment affects all players.
Use individual feedback when:
Only one player requires correction.
Confidence may be affected.
Technical adjustments are minor.
Public praise.
Private correction.
This simple principle strengthens relationships.

sections.title: Non-Verbal Communication
sections.content:
Players constantly observe their coach.
Your body language communicates before your words.
Consider:
Facial expressions.
Eye contact.
Walking pace.
Hand gestures.
Tone of voice.
Enthusiasm.
A frustrated coach creates anxious players.
A calm coach creates confident players.

sections.title: Communication During Drills
sections.content:
Avoid coaching every possession.
Instead:
Observe patterns.
Allow learning.
Intervene only when necessary.
Constant instruction creates players who look at the coach instead of scanning the field.
Football rewards independent thinkers.

sections.title: Communication During Matches
sections.content:
Match-day communication should differ from training.
Avoid:
Continuous shouting.
Repeated instructions after every possession.
Coaching every decision.
Instead:
Reinforce team principles.
Encourage.
Calm players.
Provide brief tactical reminders.
Allow players to solve problems.
Players cannot hear twenty instructions while chasing the football.

sections.title: Communicating with Different Age Groups
sections.content:

Use:

Encouragement.

Under 10

Basic questioning.
Frequent praise.

Players begin understanding:

Decision making.
Teamwork.
Ask more questions.
Provide fewer answers.
Under 14
Increase tactical discussion.
Encourage player input.
Explain the "why".
Under 16–18
Treat players as developing athletes.
Encourage ownership.
Discuss game situations.
Review decisions together.

Communicate with respect.
Players appreciate honesty.
Explain decisions.
Invite discussion.
Avoid unnecessary lectures.
Masters
Remember:
Players have work.
Families.
Injuries.
Different motivations.
Keep communication positive, efficient and enjoyable.

sections.title: Coaching Cues
sections.content:
Every skill should have short, memorable coaching cues.
Examples include:
Kicking
"Head over the ball."
"Kick through the target."
"Finish towards your teammate."
Handball
"Punch through."
"Strong platform."
"Eyes up."
Marking
"Attack the football."
"Strong hands."
"Highest point."
Ground Balls
"Low hips."
"Two hands."
"Accelerate away."
Tackling
"Eyes on the hips."
"Wrap and drive."
"Finish your feet."
The AFCRL Drill Library will reference these cues throughout every drill.

sections.title: Active Listening
sections.content:
Communication is two-way.
Good coaches:
Listen.
Observe.
Clarify.
Players often provide valuable insight into:
Fatigue.
Confusion.
Confidence.
Injuries.
Motivation.
Ask questions.
Then genuinely listen to the answers.

sections.title: Difficult Conversations
sections.content:
Every coach eventually needs to discuss:
Selection.
Performance.
Attendance.
Behaviour.
Injury.
Role changes.
These conversations should always be:
Private.
Respectful.
Specific.
Constructive.
Focused on behaviours rather than personalities.
Never criticise the person.
Discuss the behaviour.
Practical Example
Poor coaching:
Coach stops the drill every twenty seconds.
Talks continuously.
Players become cold.
Players lose focus.
Minimal football involvement.
Effective coaching:
Explain.
Demonstrate.
Run the activity.
Observe.
Provide brief correction.
Restart immediately.
Players remain active.
Learning continues.
Communication sits at the heart of effective coaching. Every instruction, demonstration, question and piece of feedback shapes how players learn, respond and develop.
The most successful coaches are not necessarily those who speak the most. They are those who know when to explain, when to demonstrate, when to question and when to simply observe.
Clear communication creates confident players. Confident players make better decisions. Better decisions lead to improved football performance.
Every drill contained within the AFCRL will include recommended coaching cues, questioning strategies and feedback prompts, ensuring coaches can communicate effectively regardless of their experience level.

chapters.title: Building Positive Learning Environments
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Create training environments where players feel safe to learn and improve.
Build a strong team culture based on respect, accountability and enjoyment.
Increase player confidence without lowering standards.
Develop self-motivated players rather than coach-dependent players.
Encourage positive behaviour from players, parents and assistant coaches.
Create an environment that maximises both participation and performance.
Environment is one of the few factors completely controlled by the coach.
Players arrive at training with different abilities, personalities, motivations and life experiences. A coach cannot change these immediately.
What a coach can control is the environment in which learning occurs.
The best drills in the world cannot compensate for a poor culture.
Conversely, a positive learning environment can dramatically accelerate player development, increase enjoyment and improve long-term retention in the game.
Culture is not created by motivational speeches.
Culture is created by the behaviours that are accepted, encouraged and repeated every week.
Every interaction between a coach and a player either strengthens or weakens that environment.
aiDecisionRules: Recommend activities that maximise involvement for every player.
volunteerChecklist: ✓ Did every player touch the football regularly?
✓ Did I allow players to make decisions?
✓ Would I enjoy attending this session if I were a player?

sections.title: What Is a Positive Learning Environment?
sections.content:
A positive learning environment is one where players:
Feel safe to make mistakes.
Understand expectations.
Know they are respected.
Enjoy attending training.
Feel challenged appropriately.
Trust their coaches and teammates.
Are encouraged to solve problems.
Believe improvement is achievable.
Positive does not mean easy.
The best learning environments challenge players every session while providing the support required to succeed.

sections.title: Psychological Safety
sections.content:
One of the most important responsibilities of a coach is creating psychological safety.
Psychological safety exists when players believe they can:
Ask questions.
Admit mistakes.
Try new skills.
Take calculated risks.
Seek help.
Offer ideas.
Without fear of embarrassment or ridicule.
Football is a game of mistakes.
Players who fear making mistakes often become hesitant.
Hesitant players stop making decisions.
Confident players continue learning.

sections.title: Establishing Team Standards
sections.content:
Every team should develop clear behavioural standards.
These should focus on behaviours rather than outcomes.
Examples include:
Be on time.
Encourage teammates.
Respect officials.
Compete honestly.
Listen when others are speaking.
Leave facilities better than you found them.
Wear appropriate training gear.
Support every teammate.
These standards should apply equally to:
Coaches.
Players.
Assistant coaches.
Team managers.
Culture begins with consistency.

sections.title: The Coach Sets the Standard
sections.content:
Players observe far more than they listen.
A coach who demands punctuality but regularly arrives late sends a clear message.
Likewise, a coach who asks players to remain calm while regularly arguing with umpires teaches the opposite behaviour.
The standard expected from players must first be demonstrated by the coaching staff.

sections.title: Encouraging Effort Over Outcome
sections.content:
Effort is always within a player's control.
Results often are not.
Reward behaviours such as:
Chasing.
Supporting teammates.
Communicating.
Competing.
Recovering after mistakes.
Trying new skills.
When coaches consistently recognise effort, players become more willing to challenge themselves.

sections.title: Mistakes as Learning Opportunities
sections.content:
Every player will make mistakes.
The question is not whether mistakes occur.
The question is how the coach responds.
Poor response:
"How many times have I told you?"
Better response:
"What did you see?"
"What could you try next time?"
"What did you learn?"
Mistakes should become discussions rather than punishments.

sections.title: Confidence and Challenge
sections.content:
Learning occurs when challenge slightly exceeds current ability.
Too little challenge creates boredom.
Too much challenge creates frustration.
The coach's role is to continually adjust activities so players experience:
Success.
Challenge.
Success.
Challenge.
This cycle builds confidence over time.

sections.title: Inclusion
sections.content:
Every player deserves meaningful involvement.
This includes:
New players.
Less experienced players.
Highly talented players.
Quiet personalities.
Confident personalities.
Avoid allowing stronger players to dominate every activity.
Rotate partners.
Rotate groups.
Rotate leadership opportunities.
Every player should feel they contribute to the team.

sections.title: Developing Leadership
sections.content:
Leadership is not restricted to captains.
Every player should be encouraged to demonstrate leadership through behaviours such as:
Helping set up training.
Collecting footballs.
Encouraging teammates.
Demonstrating drills.
Leading warm-ups.
Welcoming new players.
Leadership grows through opportunity rather than titles.

sections.title: Building Accountability
sections.content:
Accountability should be positive rather than punitive.
Encourage players to take ownership by asking:
"What was your role?"
"What could you improve?"
"What did you do well?"
Avoid immediately providing every answer.
Players who evaluate themselves become more independent.

sections.title: Competition at Training
sections.content:
Competition increases engagement.
However, poorly managed competition can reduce confidence.
Healthy competition should reward:
Teamwork.
Decision making.
Improvement.
Communication.
Effort.
Not simply winning.
Example:
Award points for:
Good communication.
Effective shepherds.
Supporting runs.
Defensive pressure.
This reinforces desired behaviours.

sections.title: Creating Enjoyment
sections.content:
Enjoyment is not the opposite of hard work.
Players enjoy training when they experience:
Improvement.
Challenge.
Success.
Belonging.
Competition.
Variety.
Purpose.
Fun games have a place within training.
So do demanding activities.
The balance depends on the age and objectives of the team.

sections.title: Working with Parents
sections.content:
Parents are essential partners in junior football.
Successful coaches communicate regularly.
Explain:
Training expectations.
Selection philosophy.
Behaviour standards.
Volunteer requirements.
Season goals.
Clear communication reduces misunderstanding.
Never criticise players through parents.
Discuss concerns directly with the player whenever appropriate.

sections.title: Assistant Coaches
sections.content:
Every assistant coach should understand:
Session objectives.
Coaching language.
Behaviour expectations.
Progressions.
Safety requirements.
Mixed coaching messages create confusion.
Consistency develops confidence.

sections.title: Handling Mistakes During Competition
sections.content:
During matches:
Avoid reacting emotionally.
Instead:
Observe.
Identify patterns.
Provide brief coaching.
Allow players to respond.
Players often solve problems more effectively than coaches expect.
Practical Example
Training Environment A
Coach criticises mistakes.
Stops drills constantly.
Only praises talented players.
Players become cautious.
Communication decreases.
Learning slows.
Training Environment B
Coach encourages experimentation.
Corrects respectfully.
Recognises effort.
Allows players to solve problems.
Players communicate more.
Confidence grows.
Learning accelerates.
A positive learning environment does not happen by accident. It is deliberately created through the behaviours, expectations and relationships established by the coach.
When players feel respected, supported and appropriately challenged, they become more willing to communicate, experiment and improve. These environments produce not only better footballers, but also more confident teammates and lifelong participants in Australian Football.
Every drill and session within the AFCRL should contribute to this environment by promoting engagement, decision making, inclusion and continuous improvement.
Coach's Reflection
Before leaving every training session, ask one final question:
"If I were one of my players, would I be excited to come back next week?"
If the answer is consistently yes, the environment you are creating is likely supporting both enjoyment and development.

chapters.title: Managing Behaviour, Discipline and Team Standards
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Establish clear behavioural expectations for players.
Build a disciplined team without relying on fear or punishment.
Create team standards that support long-term success.
Manage behaviour from players, parents and coaching staff.
The only difference is whether those standards are intentional or accidental.
Behaviour that is ignored quickly becomes accepted.
Behaviour that is consistently reinforced becomes culture.
Many coaches believe discipline means punishment.
In reality, discipline is about creating predictable expectations and helping players understand the behaviours required to contribute positively to the team.
The aim is not to control players.
The aim is to help players make good decisions independently.
When everyone understands the standards, coaches spend less time managing behaviour and more time coaching football.
aiDecisionRules: Focus on behaviours that strengthen the team environment.
volunteerChecklist: ✓ Am I discussing behaviour rather than personality?
✓ Will this conversation improve the player?
✓ Is my response consistent with previous situations?
✓ Would I be comfortable if another coach handled me this way?
Ignoring minor issues until they become major problems.
Correcting players publicly when a private conversation would be more effective.
Punishing effort mistakes rather than behavioural choices.
Allowing talented players to operate under different standards.
Making emotional decisions immediately after matches.
Every AFCRL team is encouraged to establish standards in the following areas:

sections.title: Team Standards vs Team Rules
sections.content:
Many teams begin the season by creating a list of rules.
Examples include:
Don't be late.
Don't swear.
Don't argue with umpires.
Wear the correct uniform.
Rules tell players what not to do.
Standards describe the behaviours the team values.
For example:
Instead of:
Don't be late.
Use:
We arrive early so we can prepare together.
Instead of:
Don't abuse umpires.
Use:
We show respect to everyone involved in the game.
Standards create ownership.
Rules often create resistance.

sections.title: The AFCRL Behaviour Model
sections.content:
Every behaviour should be assessed against three questions:
Does it help the player?
Does it help the team?
Does it reflect our club values?
If the answer to any question is "No", the behaviour should be addressed.
This model provides an objective framework for discussions rather than relying on emotion.

sections.title: Setting Expectations Early
sections.content:
The beginning of the season is the easiest time to establish standards.
Players should know exactly what is expected regarding:
Attendance.
Punctuality.
Effort.
Communication.
Respect.
Training intensity.
Match preparation.
Equipment.
Recovery.
Social behaviour.
Do not assume players already know.
Explain the expectations clearly.

sections.title: Consistency
sections.content:
Consistency is more important than severity.
Players quickly recognise inconsistency.
If one player is corrected for arriving late while another is ignored, the standard loses credibility.
Apply expectations fairly regardless of:
Ability.
Age.
Popularity.
Experience.
Leadership position.
Consistency builds trust.

sections.title: Positive Reinforcement
sections.content:
The behaviours that receive attention are often repeated.
Rather than focusing only on mistakes, actively recognise behaviours that strengthen the team.
Examples include:
Helping pack up equipment.
Supporting injured teammates.
Excellent communication.
Selfless running.
Strong effort.
Leadership.
Recognition does not need to be elaborate.
Simple acknowledgement is often sufficient.

sections.title: Correcting Behaviour
sections.content:
When behaviour requires correction, focus on the behaviour rather than the person.
Poor example:
"You're lazy."
Better example:
"You stopped working defensively after losing possession."
Describe:
What happened.
Why it matters.
What needs to change.
Avoid labels.
Coach behaviours.
Not personalities.

sections.title: Managing Emotional Moments
sections.content:
Football is emotional.
Mistakes.
Selection disappointment.
Poor umpiring.
Losses.
Conflict.
Coaches should remain composed.
When emotions rise:
Lower your voice.
Slow the conversation.
Ask questions.
Listen.
Avoid responding in anger.
Emotional decisions often become poor decisions.

sections.title: Conflict Between Players
sections.content:
Conflict is inevitable.
Handled well, it can strengthen relationships.
Handled poorly, it damages culture.
When conflict occurs:
Separate emotion from behaviour.
Allow each player to explain their perspective.
Focus on solutions.
Re-establish team standards.
Confirm expectations moving forward.
Never allow personal conflict to continue unchecked.

sections.title: Accountability
sections.content:
Accountability is ownership.
Players should be encouraged to evaluate themselves before receiving feedback.
Examples:
"What went well today?"
"What could you improve?"
"What would you do differently?"
Self-reflection develops independent athletes.

sections.title: Consequences
sections.content:
Consequences should be:
Relevant.
Consistent.
Educational.
Proportionate.
Avoid punishment that has no connection to the behaviour.
Example:
Late arrival.
Appropriate consequence:
Player helps set up equipment next session.
Poor consequence:
Twenty push-ups.
The purpose is learning.
Not embarrassment.

sections.title: Discipline During Training
sections.content:
Avoid stopping the entire session because one player loses concentration.
Instead:
Move closer.
Use eye contact.
Ask a question.
Provide a reminder.
If required, speak privately.
Maintain training flow wherever possible.
The behaviour of one player should not unnecessarily reduce learning opportunities for the rest of the group.

sections.title: Discipline During Matches
sections.content:
Emotion often increases on game day.
Coaches should avoid:
Public criticism.
Sarcasm.
Personal attacks.
Continuous negative commentary.
Instead:
Provide clear instructions.
Reinforce team principles.
Encourage effort.
Review decisions after the match rather than during emotional moments.

sections.title: Managing Parents
sections.content:
Most parents want the same thing coaches want:
Children who enjoy football and improve.
Communication reduces conflict.
Provide information about:
Selection.
Playing time philosophy.
Training expectations.
Behaviour standards.
Volunteer opportunities.
If concerns arise:
Listen respectfully.
Discuss privately.
Remain calm.
Focus on the player.
Avoid arguments immediately after games.

sections.title: Assistant Coaches
sections.content:
Assistant coaches should model the same standards expected from players.
This includes:
Respect.
Language.
Professionalism.
Preparation.
Communication.
Disagreements should occur privately.
Players should see a united coaching group.

sections.title: Social Media
sections.content:
Players increasingly represent their club beyond the football field.
Encourage respectful online behaviour.
Remind players:
Posts are public.
Screenshots last forever.
Respect teammates.
Respect opponents.
Respect officials.
The standards expected on the field should continue online.

sections.title: When Standards Are Breached
sections.content:
Follow a consistent process.
Step 1
Identify the behaviour.
Step 2
Discuss privately.
Step 3
Explain why it matters.
Step 4
Agree on improvement.
Step 5
Follow up.
This process should remain calm and respectful.
The objective is behavioural improvement rather than punishment.
Practical Example
Scenario
A player repeatedly arrives ten minutes late to training.
Poor response:
Public criticism.
Embarrassment.
Punishment in front of teammates.
Likely outcome:
Reduced motivation.
Damaged relationship.
Effective response:
Private conversation.
Ask why.
Listen.
Explain team expectations.
Agree on a solution.
Review next week.
Likely outcome:
Ownership.
Respect.
Improved behaviour.
Discipline is not about control. It is about creating an environment where players understand what is expected, accept responsibility for their behaviour and contribute positively to the team.
The most effective coaches establish standards early, apply them consistently and respond to challenges calmly and respectfully. By focusing on behaviours rather than personalities, coaches develop accountable players who take ownership of both their football and their contribution to the team.
Strong standards create strong cultures, and strong cultures allow coaches to spend more time developing footballers and less time managing behaviour.
Coach's Reflection
Ask yourself regularly:
"Do my players behave well because they fear consequences, or because they genuinely understand and believe in our team standards?"
Teams built on understanding will almost always outperform teams built on fear over the long term.

Volume 1 – Foundations of Coaching Australian Football

chapters.title: Training Load, Player Welfare and Injury Prevention
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Understand the importance of balancing training, competition and recovery.
Recognise the signs of physical and mental fatigue.
Plan training sessions that maximise development while reducing unnecessary injury risk.
Modify training loads for different age groups and playing groups.
Promote player welfare throughout the football season.
Understand the coach's role in injury prevention.
Develop training environments that place player wellbeing ahead of short-term results.
Every coach wants players to improve.
Improvement, however, is not simply the result of training harder.

Players improve when training places an appropriate level of stress on the body and mind, followed by adequate recovery. Too little training produces minimal improvement, while excessive training increases fatigue, decreases performance and significantly increases the risk of injury.

Community football presents additional challenges. Players often balance football with school, work, family commitments and other sports. Unlike professional athletes, recovery time is limited and training opportunities are fewer.
For this reason, community coaches must carefully balance the demands of training with the realities of everyday life.
The objective is not to see how hard players can train.
The objective is to ensure players are healthy, motivated and available to participate consistently throughout the season.
aiDecisionRules: When recommending training sessions, the AFCRL AI Coaching System should:
Match training load to the age and development of the players.
Reduce training intensity during extreme weather.
Flag drills with high physical or contact demands.
Modify activities for injured or returning players.
Prioritise long-term player welfare over short-term performance.
Recommend adequate hydration opportunities during all sessions.
volunteerChecklist: Before every training session ask yourself:
✓ Have I planned a proper warm-up?
✓ Have I checked the playing surface?
✓ Do I know which players are carrying injuries?
✓ Have I considered today's weather conditions?
✓ Is the session appropriate for the age group?
✓ Do I have a first aid kit available?
✓ Have I planned an appropriate cool-down?
Running excessive conditioning without the football.
Failing to adjust training during extreme weather.
Believing harder training always produces better performance.

sections.title: The Coach's Responsibility
sections.content:
One of the coach's primary responsibilities is protecting the welfare of every player.
This responsibility extends beyond teaching football skills.
A coach should strive to provide an environment that is:
Safe.
Enjoyable.
Challenging.
Inclusive.
Appropriate for the age and ability of the players.
Winning a match should never come at the expense of a player's long-term health.
Good coaches always place player welfare ahead of short-term success.

sections.title: Understanding Training Load
sections.content:
Training load refers to the total demands placed on a player during football activities.
These demands are not limited to running distance.
Training load includes:
Running volume.
Sprint efforts.
Accelerations and decelerations.
Physical contact.
Repeated contests.
Technical skill repetition.
Decision making.
Concentration.
Emotional stress.
Two training sessions may last exactly ninety minutes but create completely different levels of fatigue.
The quality and intensity of activities are often more important than their duration.

sections.title: External Load
sections.content:
External load describes the work completed by the player.
Examples include:
Distance covered.
Number of sprints.
Number of kicks.
Number of handballs.
Number of contests.
Tackles performed.
Time spent training.
Professional clubs use GPS systems to monitor these measures.
Community coaches can estimate external load by observing the intensity and structure of each activity.

sections.title: Internal Load
sections.content:
Internal load describes how difficult the session feels to the player.
It is influenced by many factors, including:
Fitness.
Sleep quality.
Nutrition.
Illness.
Stress.
Previous training.
Weather conditions.
Recovery from previous matches.
Two players completing the same drill may experience very different internal loads.
For this reason, coaches should regularly communicate with players and encourage honest feedback regarding fatigue and recovery.

sections.title: Recognising Fatigue
sections.content:
Fatigue affects both physical performance and decision making.
Common signs include:
Slower movement.
Reduced work rate.
Poor skill execution.
Slower reactions.
Reduced communication.
Poor concentration.
Frustration.
Negative body language.
Difficulty following instructions.
When several of these signs appear together, coaches should consider modifying the session.
Reducing intensity early is often preferable to allowing fatigue to continue increasing.

sections.title: Recovery
sections.content:
Recovery is where improvement occurs.
Training creates stress.
Recovery allows the body and mind to adapt.
Without adequate recovery, players accumulate fatigue rather than fitness.
Encourage players to prioritise:
Quality sleep.
Hydration.
Nutritious meals.
Gentle movement after matches.
Recovery between training sessions.
Recovery should be viewed as an essential part of training rather than an optional extra.

sections.title: Age-Specific Training Loads
sections.content:
Training loads should always reflect the age and development of the players.
Under 8–Under 10
The emphasis should remain on:
Enjoyment.
Skill development.
Movement.
Participation.
Avoid prolonged conditioning activities without the football.
Under 12–Under 14
Gradually increase training intensity while maintaining a strong focus on skill development.
Players experiencing rapid growth may fatigue more quickly and require additional recovery.
Under 16–Under 18
Training intensity can increase significantly.
Coaches should remain aware of school commitments, representative football and periods of rapid physical development.
Senior Football
Adult players often balance football with employment and family responsibilities.
Training should be demanding but efficient.
Recovery requirements differ greatly between individuals.
Masters Football
Recovery should receive equal importance to training.
Training should remain competitive while minimising unnecessary physical overload.
Warm-ups become increasingly important with age.

sections.title: Injury Prevention
sections.content:
Although injuries cannot be eliminated completely, coaches can reduce unnecessary risk through sensible planning.
Before every session:
Inspect the playing surface.
Remove hazards.
Check footballs and equipment.
Ensure first aid equipment is available.
Confirm emergency procedures are understood.
Plan an appropriate warm-up.
Players should never begin intense football activities without adequate preparation.

sections.title: Warm-Ups
sections.content:
Every training session should begin with a structured warm-up.
An effective warm-up prepares players physically and mentally for the activities ahead.
Warm-ups should include:
Light running.
Dynamic mobility.
Acceleration.
Change of direction.
Football-specific movement.
Ball involvement.
Warm-ups should gradually increase in intensity.
Static stretching alone is not an adequate football warm-up.

sections.title: Cool-Downs
sections.content:
Following training, players should gradually reduce their activity level.
Cool-down activities may include:
Walking.
Light jogging.
Mobility exercises.
Team review.
The cool-down also provides an opportunity for coaches to reinforce key learning points while players recover.

sections.title: Managing Injured Players
sections.content:
Injured players remain valuable members of the team.
Whenever appropriate, they should continue participating in non-physical ways.
Examples include:
Assisting coaches.
Recording statistics.
Demonstrating drills.
Helping with equipment.
Supporting teammates.
Maintaining involvement helps preserve team connection and motivation during rehabilitation.

sections.title: Concussion Awareness
sections.content:
Any suspected concussion should be treated seriously.
If concussion is suspected:
Remove the player from participation immediately.
Do not allow the player to return on the same day.
Ensure appropriate medical assessment occurs.
Follow competition and medical return-to-play guidelines.
Player health always takes priority over football.

sections.title: Hydration
sections.content:
Hydration should be planned rather than left to chance.
Coaches should schedule regular drink breaks, particularly during:
Hot weather.
High humidity.
Longer training sessions.
High-intensity activities.
Players should be encouraged to arrive well hydrated before training begins.

sections.title: Heat and Environmental Conditions
sections.content:
Environmental conditions should always influence session planning.
During extreme heat:
Reduce drill duration.
Increase recovery periods.
Provide additional hydration breaks.
Use shaded areas where available.
Monitor players carefully.
During storms or unsafe conditions, training should be modified or postponed in accordance with local competition policies.
Player safety must always remain the priority.

sections.title: Balancing Football and Life
sections.content:
Community footballers have commitments beyond football.
These may include:
School.
University.
Work.
Family.
Other sports.
Effective coaches understand these competing demands and communicate openly with players.
Supporting player wellbeing contributes to greater long-term participation and improved performance.
Practical Example
A senior player arrives at training after completing a physically demanding twelve-hour work shift.
Rather than expecting identical performance to every other player, the coach speaks privately with the player before training.
Together they decide the player will complete the football-specific components of the session while reducing unnecessary running volume.
The player remains engaged, contributes positively and reduces the likelihood of excessive fatigue before the weekend's match.
Good coaching considers the individual rather than applying identical expectations to every player.
Training load management is one of the most important responsibilities of every coach. Effective player development depends not only on providing appropriate challenges but also on ensuring players recover sufficiently between training sessions and matches.
By recognising fatigue, planning appropriate workloads and placing player welfare first, coaches create environments where players remain healthy, motivated and available to improve throughout the season.
Successful football teams are built through consistent participation, intelligent planning and a genuine commitment to protecting the wellbeing of every player.
Coach's Reflection
Before planning your next training session, ask yourself:
"Will today's session make my players better, or simply make them more tired?"
The most effective coaches understand the difference.

Australian Football Coaching Reference Library (AFCRL)
Volume 1 – Foundations of Coaching Australian Football

chapters.title: Building a Season Plan
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Understand the importance of long-term planning.
Develop a season plan appropriate to their team and competition.
Identify key phases of the football season.
Progress player development logically throughout the year.
Balance skill development, tactical learning and physical preparation.
Adapt season plans to changing circumstances.
Evaluate team progress throughout the season.
Successful football teams are rarely built from one good training session.
They are built through months of consistent planning, purposeful coaching and gradual improvement.
Many coaches plan only one week ahead. While this approach may work in the short term, it often results in repetitive training, rushed preparation and important skills being overlooked.
It allows coaches to identify where the team currently sits, where they want the team to be at the end of the season and the most effective path to reach that destination.
A season plan should remain flexible.
Unexpected injuries, weather, player availability and competition scheduling will all require adjustments throughout the year.
The purpose of planning is not to predict the future perfectly.
The purpose is to ensure every training session contributes to long-term player and team development.
aiDecisionRules: When generating season plans, the AFCRL AI Coaching System should:
Progress skills logically throughout the year.
Balance technical, tactical and physical development.
Adapt recommendations to player age and competition level.
Schedule recovery following periods of high training load.
Recommend flexibility when unexpected disruptions occur.
Align every training session with long-term development objectives.
volunteerChecklist: Changing the game plan every week.
Introducing too many new concepts simultaneously.

sections.title: Why Plan an Entire Season?
sections.content:
Planning provides clarity.
Rather than asking each week:
"What should we do at training tonight?"
The coach already knows:
What the team is learning.
Why it is being taught.
What comes next.
How progress will be measured.
Season planning also prevents important areas of football from being neglected.
Every major skill and tactical concept should appear repeatedly throughout the year.

sections.title: The Four Phases of the Season
sections.content:
For most community football clubs, the season can be divided into four phases.
Phase 1 – Pre-Season
Primary Objectives:
Build fitness.
Establish team culture.
Introduce the game plan.
Develop fundamental skills.
Prepare players physically.
Training emphasis:
High skill repetition.
Progressive conditioning.
Team standards.
Ball movement fundamentals.
Phase 2 – Early Season
Primary Objectives:
Transfer training into matches.
Build consistency.
Continue skill development.
Reinforce team structures.
Training emphasis:
Match scenarios.
Decision making.
Team communication.
Game review.
Phase 3 – Mid Season
Primary Objectives:
Refine performance.
Address weaknesses.
Maintain player health.
Continue tactical development.
Training emphasis:
Football-specific conditioning.
Opposition preparation.
Skill maintenance.
Recovery.
Phase 4 – Finals Preparation
Primary Objectives:
Maintain confidence.
Maximise freshness.
Reinforce strengths.
Prepare mentally.
Training emphasis:
Match intensity.
Short, sharp sessions.
Team cohesion.
Role clarity.

sections.title: Establishing Team Goals
sections.content:
Every season should begin with clearly defined goals.
Goals should be divided into three categories.
Player Development Goals
Examples:
Improve kicking accuracy.
Increase confidence.
Develop leadership.
Improve decision making.
Team Performance Goals
Examples:
Improve defensive transition.
Increase uncontested marks.
Reduce turnovers.
Improve scoring efficiency.
Cultural Goals
Examples:
Excellent attendance.
Positive communication.
Respect for officials.
Strong teamwork.
Not every goal should involve winning matches.
Development remains the priority.

sections.title: Weekly Planning
sections.content:
Each week should build upon the previous one.
Example:
Week 1
Introduce defensive positioning.
↓
Week 2
Pressure around the contest.
↓
Week 3
Defensive transition.
↓
Week 4
Game simulation.
Rather than treating every week independently, coaches should progressively develop concepts over time.

sections.title: Balancing Skill Development
sections.content:
Throughout the season, every major football skill should receive regular attention.
These include:
Kicking.
Handball.
Marking.
Ground balls.
Tackling.
Goal kicking.
Ball movement.
Transition.
Team defence.
Decision making.
Communication.
Even experienced teams benefit from revisiting fundamental skills.

sections.title: Match Review
sections.content:
Every match provides valuable information.
Following each game, coaches should review:
What worked well?
What needs improvement?
What should be reinforced?
What should become the focus of next week's training?
The purpose of review is improvement rather than criticism.

sections.title: Flexibility
sections.content:
No season unfolds exactly as planned.
Coaches should expect:
Injuries.
Wet weather.
Low attendance.
Representative football.
Ground closures.
Fixture changes.
Good season plans allow flexibility without abandoning long-term objectives.

sections.title: Individual Player Development
sections.content:
Not every player progresses at the same rate.
Coaches should identify:
Players requiring additional confidence.
Players ready for greater challenges.
Leadership opportunities.
Position changes.
Skill priorities.
Every player should experience individual development throughout the season.

sections.title: Managing Workload
sections.content:
Training intensity should fluctuate throughout the year.
Periods of heavy learning and high intensity should be balanced with recovery.
Avoid attempting to improve every aspect of football simultaneously.
Progressive development produces better long-term results.

sections.title: Evaluating Progress
sections.content:
Regular evaluation keeps the season on track.
Questions coaches should ask include:
Are players improving?
Are training objectives being achieved?
Is attendance remaining strong?
Are players enjoying football?
Has team communication improved?
Are skills transferring into matches?
Evaluation should occur throughout the season rather than only at its conclusion.
Practical Example
A coach identifies that their Under 14 team struggles moving the football from defence.
Rather than running random kicking drills each week, they develop a four-week progression.
Week One:
Defensive positioning.
Week Two:
Short kicking options.
Week Three:
Transition through the corridor.
Week Four:
Full-ground defensive exit simulation.
Each week builds naturally upon the previous week's learning.
A successful football season is built through deliberate planning rather than weekly improvisation. Coaches who establish clear objectives, progressively develop players and regularly evaluate performance create environments where consistent improvement becomes possible.
A season plan should remain flexible enough to respond to changing circumstances while maintaining a clear long-term direction. Every training session, every match and every review should contribute to the team's ongoing development.
Coach's Reflection
Before finalising your season plan, ask yourself:
"If every training session goes exactly as planned, what will my players be able to do in six months that they cannot do today?"
The answer should describe measurable improvement in both individual players and the team as a whole.

chapters.title: The AFCRL Coaching Toolkit
learningObjectives: After completing this chapter, coaches should be able to:
Identify the essential equipment required to conduct effective training sessions.
Prepare training sessions efficiently using the AFCRL Coaching Toolkit.
Understand the purpose of each coaching aid.
Organise equipment to maximise player participation.
Utilise technology appropriately to support coaching and player development.
Maintain coaching equipment throughout the season.
Develop consistent preparation habits before every training session.
Good coaches prepare before players arrive.
Well-organised training sessions rarely happen by chance. They are the result of thoughtful planning, appropriate equipment and efficient organisation.
A coach does not need expensive technology to deliver outstanding training. Many of the best community coaches achieve excellent results using only footballs, cones and clear communication.
However, the right equipment allows coaches to spend less time organising activities and more time developing players.
The AFCRL Coaching Toolkit provides a practical checklist of equipment and resources that support effective coaching at every level of Australian Football.
The aim is not to own every available coaching aid.
The aim is to have the right equipment available to deliver safe, engaging and purposeful training sessions.
aiDecisionRules: When recommending coaching resources, the AFCRL AI Coaching System should:
Prioritise simple equipment that maximises player involvement.
Recommend technology only when it improves coaching efficiency.
Match equipment recommendations to player age and session objectives.
Suggest alternative equipment when standard resources are unavailable.
Minimise equipment requirements where possible to support volunteer coaches.
volunteerChecklist: Arriving at the same time as players.
Beginning training before equipment is organised.
Using equipment without a clear purpose.
Running out of footballs during drills.

sections.title: Essential Coaching Equipment
sections.content:
Every coach should have access to the following equipment.
Footballs
The most important piece of equipment.
Ideally:
One football for every two players during skill activities.
Additional footballs available for continuous drills.
Cones
Used to:
Define playing areas.
Mark starting positions.
Create gates.
Establish boundaries.
Build running patterns.
A minimum of 40 cones is recommended.
Bibs
Used to identify:
Teams.
Attackers and defenders.
Floating players.
Positional groups.
Multiple colours improve organisation.
Whistle
Useful for:
Starting activities.
Stopping activities.
Safety situations.
The whistle should support communication, not replace it.
Stopwatch
Useful for:
Drill timing.
Work-to-rest ratios.
Session management.
Players remain engaged when activities operate to consistent time limits.

sections.title: Recommended Coaching Equipment
sections.content:
Although not essential, the following equipment can significantly improve training.
Examples include:
Agility poles.
Hit shields.
Mini goals.
Marker discs.
Boundary markers.
Resistance bands.
Hurdles.
Speed ladders.
Whiteboard.
Magnetic coaching board.
Each item should have a clear coaching purpose.
Equipment should never be introduced simply for variety.

sections.title: First Aid Equipment
sections.content:
Every training session should have immediate access to:
First aid kit.
Ice packs.
Disposable gloves.
Emergency contact information.
Mobile phone.
Coaches should know who is responsible for first aid before training begins.

sections.title: Preparing the Training Area
sections.content:
Players should arrive to a training environment that is ready to begin.
Before training:
Position cones.
Inflate footballs.
Prepare bibs.
Check goals.
Inspect the ground.
Remove hazards.
Preparation before players arrive significantly increases active training time.

sections.title: Whiteboards and Visual Learning
sections.content:
Many players learn more effectively through visual instruction.
Whiteboards can be used to explain:
Team structures.
Ball movement.
Kick-in strategies.
Centre bounce setups.
Defensive positioning.
Keep diagrams simple.
Players should understand the message within a few seconds.

sections.title: Video
sections.content:
Video can be a valuable learning tool when used appropriately.
Examples include:
Recording skill technique.
Reviewing team structures.
Demonstrating successful examples.
Comparing before and after performance.
Video should reinforce learning rather than replace coaching.
Avoid overwhelming players with excessive footage.

sections.title: Technology
sections.content:
Technology should simplify coaching rather than complicate it.
Useful examples include:
Session planning applications.
Digital whiteboards.
Training attendance systems.
GPS units (where available).
Video analysis software.
AI coaching assistants.
Technology should always support coaching decisions rather than make them.

sections.title: Session Planning Resources
sections.content:
Every coach should maintain a record of:
Training plans.
Drill library.
Attendance.
Injuries.
Player development notes.
Match observations.
Recording information helps coaches identify long-term trends rather than relying on memory.

sections.title: Equipment Management
sections.content:
After every training session:
Count footballs.
Collect cones.
Wash bibs.
Store equipment correctly.
Replace damaged items.
Recharge electronic devices.
Looking after equipment reduces unnecessary costs and improves training efficiency.

sections.title: Organising Equipment During Training
sections.content:
Equipment should be positioned so that transitions between drills are quick.
Where possible:
Set up the next activity before finishing the current one.
Use assistant coaches to prepare stations.
Minimise unnecessary walking.
Keep spare footballs around the training area.
Players should spend their time learning rather than waiting for equipment.

sections.title: Coaching Resources
sections.content:
Every coach should continue developing their own knowledge.
Useful resources include:
AFL coaching courses.
Club coaching mentors.
Match observation.
Coaching books.
Video analysis.
Professional development workshops.
Personal coaching reflection.
The best coaches never stop learning.
Practical Example
A coach arrives thirty minutes before training.
Before players arrive they:
Inspect the oval.
Set out cones.
Inflate footballs.
Prepare bibs.
Write the session objectives on the whiteboard.
Organise the first drill.
When players arrive, training begins immediately.
As a result:
Players remain engaged.
Explanations are shorter.
More football is completed.
Coaches spend less time organising equipment.
Preparation creates efficiency.
The quality of a training session is heavily influenced by the coach's preparation. Appropriate equipment, organised resources and thoughtful planning allow players to spend more time learning and less time waiting.
The AFCRL Coaching Toolkit is designed to support coaches at every level by providing practical, affordable and effective resources that improve organisation, communication and player development.
Good coaching does not depend on expensive equipment.
It depends on using the right equipment in the right way.
Coach's Reflection
Before leaving for your next training session, ask yourself:
"Have I prepared everything my players need to succeed before they arrive?"
Well-prepared coaches create well-organised training environments, and well-organised training environments create better learning opportunities.
